overview: Joseon ruled Korea for more than five centuries under a Neo-Confucian order. King Sejong's court gave the country its alphabet, Hangul, and a run of scientific instruments; the dynasty survived Japanese and Manchu invasions and lasted, as the Korean Empire after 1897, until Japan annexed it in 1910.

items.text: King Sejong created Hangul, published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, so that ordinary people could read and write.
The cheugugi rain gauge, a standard cylinder read against a ruler, was set up across the provinces, nearly two centuries before the first European rain gauge of 1639.
Jang Yeong-sil's self-striking water clock, the Jagyeongnu, and armillary spheres and sundials for the royal observatory.
The Chiljeongsan calendar reform computed the motions of the sun, moon and planets for Seoul's own meridian.
Heo Jun's Donguibogam, a medical encyclopedia, was published.
White porcelain, plain or painted in cobalt blue, became the ware of the scholar's table.
The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, a daily record of every reign from 1392 to 1863, among the longest continuous histories in the world.
Neo-Confucianism became state orthodoxy; Buddhism lost its land and court standing.
Civil service examinations on the Confucian classics selected officials, and the yangban scholar class ran the state.
Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships and cannon fleets cut the Japanese supply lines during the invasions of 1592 to 1598.
Gunpowder weapons, from hwacha rocket carts to ship-borne cannon, were made at state arsenals.
Hangul is the writing system of both Koreas today.
Neo-Confucian family and social values shaped Korean life for centuries.

fall.text: Joseon was proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897 under the same royal house. Japan made it a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910.
